\section[\hi{सुप्रभात}]{\hi{सुप्रभात} (suprabhāt) — "good morning," a different root than the noun}

\label{lesson:HI-C31-suprabhat}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} \hi{सुबह} was Persian, borrowed whole. This lesson's "good morning" isn't built on it at all — it reaches for entirely different, native vocabulary.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{सुप्रभात}}
\textbf{\hi{सुप्रभात}} (\textbf{suprabhāt}) — "\textbf{good morning}" — is built from \textbf{\hi{सु}} (\emph{su}, "good") plus \textbf{\hi{प्रभात}} (\emph{prabhāta}, "\textbf{dawn, daybreak}") — and \emph{prabhāta} is \textbf{native Sanskrit}, from \textbf{\hi{प्रभा}} (\emph{prabhā}, "light, splendour"), itself from the root \textbf{\hi{भा}} ("to shine") plus the preverb \textbf{\hi{प्र}-} ("forth"), plus the suffix \emph{\textbf{-\hi{त}}} (\emph{-ta}). This is a \textbf{completely different word} from \textbf{\hi{सुबह}} (\emph{subah}, HI-C28), the Persian/Arabic loan you use for the everyday noun "morning." Hindi's "morning" and "good morning" don't share a root at all.

\subsection*{The exchange — Formal register}
Here's a genuine, checked-not-assumed finding — hedged carefully, since this arc's earlier lesson (Telugu's TE-C25) only ever offered a similarly hedged claim itself: some sources describe Telugu speakers often code-switching to English "good night" instead of their own Sanskrit-descended phrase, though even that lesson admitted the evidence was thin and might apply more broadly across South Asian languages, not just Telugu. \hi{सुप्रभात}'s own story is different again, and just as worth hedging: it skews toward \textbf{formal, written} contexts — speeches, radio, the well-known Hindi WhatsApp-forward "good morning image" culture — rather than casual spoken conversation, where \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}} commonly covers mornings too. That's a real formal/everyday split, but it isn't the same thing as being displaced by \textbf{English} specifically — there's no strong evidence for that particular substitution here. Don't assume every "good \_\_\_" greeting in every language this course covers follows the same displacement story; verify each one on its own, and don't flatten a hedge into a fact either way.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Does \hi{सुप्रभात} share a root with \hi{सुबह}? (\textbf{No} — \hi{सुबह} is Persian/Arabic; \hi{प्रभात}, inside suprabhāt, is native Sanskrit, ultimately from \hi{भा}, "to shine.") Is \hi{सुप्रभात} commonly used in casual spoken Hindi? (\textbf{Not especially} — it skews formal/written, with \hi{नमस्ते} commonly covering mornings in everyday speech.) Is it being displaced by English "good morning," the way some sources (thinly) suggested for other languages' night greetings in this arc? (\textbf{No strong evidence of that} — its own story is a formal/everyday split, not an English substitution.)
\end{tcolorbox}
